articles.summary: Global oil prices dipped after US leadership signaled that further direct military conflict with Iran was unlikely amid ongoing diplomatic efforts.
articles.explain: Oil prices are determined by global supply and demand. When threats to shipping lanes arise, traders build a 'risk premium' into the price of oil. When those threats appear to diminish, that premium is removed, leading to a drop in price.

story.title: Global Oil Price Fluctuations
story.so_far: Oil markets are highly sensitive to geopolitical instability, particularly in the Middle East, which accounts for a significant portion of the world's oil supply. The Strait of Hormuz is a critical shipping lane; disruptions there often lead to supply concerns and price spikes, while diplomatic resolutions tend to lower prices.

timeline.text: Oil prices fell at the start of the week as geopolitical tensions regarding the Strait of Hormuz showed signs of easing.

articles.title: BoE’s Pill sees scope for interest rate cuts if UK growth stalls
articles.summary: The Bank of England's chief economist signaled that future interest rate cuts could be on the table if domestic economic growth begins to decline.
articles.explain: Interest rates represent the cost of borrowing money. If an economy is 'stalling,' a central bank may cut rates to make borrowing cheaper, encouraging businesses and consumers to spend. If inflation is too high, they raise rates to slow down spending and bring prices back under control.

story.title: Bank of England Monetary Policy
story.so_far: Central banks, such as the Bank of England, use interest rates as a primary tool to manage inflation and stimulate or cool the economy. Recently, global markets have seen a push-and-pull between managing stubborn inflation and preventing a recessionary slowdown, leaving economists closely watching central bank guidance for future rate trajectories.

timeline.text: Economist Huw Pill noted potential flexibility in interest rate policy based on future UK growth indicators.

articles.title: ROI-Tin hit by AI stock rout despite physical market tightness: Andy Home
articles.summary: Despite tight supplies in the physical market, the price of tin has fallen due to the negative sentiment triggered by the broader AI stock sell-off.
articles.explain: Physical market tightness means there isn't enough of a product to meet current demand. Normally, this should push prices up. However, in modern markets, general 'risk-off' sentiment—where investors sell off assets broadly because they are worried about tech sector losses—can cause prices to drop even if a specific commodity is actually in short supply.
